newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OPINION - Zimbabwe debt vs inflation - By T.Hawkins.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Zimbabwe debt vs inflation - By T.Hawkins.

text.p: By Tony Hawkins, Professor of Business Studies at The University of Zimbabwe
When the Washington-based International Finance Corp compiles its 1996 emerging markets performance indicators, Zimbabwe will be very close to the top.

In a year in which the Zimbabwe dollar has depreciated 13% against the US dollar, the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange index of industrial share prices -- which touched a new record high of 8091 last week (Thurs 21) -- has doubled, so that in US dollar terms investors have enjoyed gains of around 90%.

Up to a point this strong performance mirrors and anticipates the economy's recovery from the 1995 drought. Real GDP is expected to grow by around 7% this year after a 2.7% decline in 1995. But the surge in industrial shares has pushed the return on equities down to a mere 2.3% while the price-earnings ratio of almost 18 is assuming first-world market proportions.

Interestingly, foreign investors had little to do with the 1996 bull run. By mid-November they had bought some Z$554 million (US$55 million) in Zimbabwe equities but sold Z$552 million, so that their net holding of Zimbabwe equity at Z$1.1 billion (US$ 110 million) was barely changed.

Foreigners were net buyers of Zimbabwe equities in the first half of the year to the tune of some Z$77 million, but purchases and sales virtually cancelled each other out in the third quarter, while in the six weeks to mid-November, offshore investors were net sellers of some Z$75 million worth of shares.

This net selling suggests that foreign investors believe the market is too high, that the Zimbabwe dollar is overvalued and poised to fall, and possibly also that foreigners see richer pickings elsewhere.

Whatever the reasons for it, recent net foreign sales underline the strength of domestic support for the equity market. Just how much of this is attributable to the upgrading of earnings and dividend prospects, rather than more straightforward monetary and yield considerations is unclear. As monetary policy has eased and interest rates declined so investors have moved into equities and, in some cases, real estate.

The resulting asset price inflation -- equities up over 100% and property prices more than 40% in the last year -- is a reminder of the potentially powerful inflationary pressures still at work in the economy.

With the central bank having abandoned its earlier policy of mopping up excess market liquidity through the issue of treasury bills and with treasury bill yields fractionally below the inflation rate of 20.2% in October, money market investments -- where they are available -- have lost their appeal.

The stock market's next move is likely to be driven by a combination of monetary considerations and the weather. With two severe droughts fresh in investors' memories, climatic conditions tend to have a strong influence in the equity market.

There are at least some signs that this is being overdone, since even if there is another relatively normal season -- as long-range forecasts suggest - the "rebound factor" that was such an important influence in the economy during 1996, will be less potent.

With the Reserve (central) Bank of Zimbabwe pursuing a contradictory policy of cutting interest rates while seeking to curb money supply growth, the future direction of monetary policy is difficult to call.

In the wake of two public service pay awards that will cost over Z$2.5 billion (US$250 million), thereby pushing the fiscal deficit to around 11% from the budget forecast of 8.5%, there is no justification for any easing of monetary policy.

Fiscal policy ought to be tightened but this is easier said than done when the authorities are battling to contain further public sector pay demands by seeking to sit out the four-week long strike by nurses and junior doctors at state hospitals.

Some tax hikes are on the cards early in the new year -- if not before -- since without them, there is little likelihood of Zimbabwe being able to reach agreement with the IMF on a new adjustment loan.
Rational economics dictates tightening both fiscal and monetary policy in the first half of 1997, but rationality has not been to the fore in a number of recent government economic decisions.

The stock market, taking its cue from the downtrend in inflation rates over the last six months and the central bank's willingness to see interest rates fall despite rapid monetary growth, may continue its bull run for some while yet.

But sooner or later the reckoning will have to come. If there is to be an IMF agreement, the budget deficit will have to be tackled vigorously which -- in the short run at least -- will be bad news for stocks, though in the medium-term, it can only have positive implications.
Whether a government that for the last six years has resolutely avoided fiscal retrenchment is now ready to turn over a new leaf is another matter.

More worryingly, given the severity of the domestic debt crisis it faces, is the possibility that the debt trap is now close to the stage where inflation is the most practical -- if not the only -- way out of the woods.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
